english_translation: Dionysius the Areopagite saw this. After all that he wrote in the Symbolic Theology, in the Theological Institutions, in On the Divine Names, and in On Mystical Theology, he finally at the end of that work spoke as he could about God in a very holy way, as if he were already in the cloud.
exegesis: Pico invokes Pseudo-Dionysius as the exemplary figure of mystical ascent within a hierarchical framework. The reference to Pseudo-Dionysius's four works—especially the progression from Symbolic Theology through Divine Names to Mystical Theology—traces a ladder of negation: from symbols (affirmative theology) through names (divine attributes) to ultimate unknowing (apophatic theology). Pico positions the nine angelic orders as the rungs of this ladder. The 'cloud' alludes to the Dionysian cloud of unknowing that surpasses even the highest angelic intellection—God's transcendence exceeds even the seraphim's participation.
metaphysical_theme: Pseudo-Dionysius's hierarchical angelology as the metaphysical framework for mystical ascent; the nine angelic orders as rungs on the ladder toward divine darkness that transcends even the highest created intellects

other_texts: Heptaplus Layer 2: Pseudo-Dionysius hierarchy explicitly mapped to the creation narrative and six days

scholar_citations: Pseudo-Dionysius, De divinis nominibus, De mystica theologia: Primary authorities on angelic hierarchy and apophatic path to God
Howlett: Pico's use of Pseudo-Dionysius as synthesis of Neoplatonic emanation and Christian mysticism

notes: HARVESTER passage U.2.1 establishes Pseudo-Dionysius as the authoritative voice for Pico's angelology. The four works form a pedagogical sequence: starting with visible symbols, ascending through abstract names and attributes, and culminating in the transnational cloud where even intellectual knowledge fails. This structure organizes all of Pico's treatment of angels across the 900 Conclusions.
